en: The kingdoms fought over copper: Kition seized Idalion in the middle of the fifth century and later bought Tamassos outright, gaining direct control of the mines, and the Phoenician administration at Idalion left more than a thousand inscribed pottery fragments, almost all of them economic records. Timber was the other strategic commodity, going into the fleets the kings supplied first to Persia and then to Alexander, a hundred and fifty ships at Salamis in 480 BCE and a hundred and twenty at the siege of Tyre in 332, and wine, oil and grain went out beside it. Each kingdom struck its own coin, in silver on a Persian standard and, from the reign of Melekiathon of Kition, in gold and bronze as well.

Greek in the Cypriot syllabary remained the standard written language, and the longest surviving syllabic text, the bronze Idalion Tablet of the mid fifth century, records King Stasikypros and the city paying a family of physicians in silver and land for treating the wounded during a siege. Phoenician was the administrative language of Kition and its dependencies, and bilingual inscriptions in Phoenician and syllabic Greek become common. Eteocypriot survived at Amathus into the fourth century, where the bilingual inscription published in 1914 gives what appears to be the same dedication in Greek and in the native tongue; the language is still undeciphered, and the Greek half is all that allows even a partial reading of the other.

The old cults continued and grew more Greek in appearance: the Paphian goddess is still Wanassa in inscriptions until the name Aphrodite appears for the first time late in the fourth century, and the kings of Paphos ruled by virtue of her priesthood. Kition's Astarte and Melqart, the Apollo-Reshef of Idalion, and Zeus Ammon in his Cypriot guise show a habit of blending rather than replacing, and Cypriot votive sculpture of the period adopts Greek poses and drapery while keeping local dress and local gods. Rock-cut chamber tombs remained the norm, and the ostentatious built tombs of the Salamis kings had already been abandoned before the period began.

Salamis was the largest city by far, holding on one estimate thirty-five to thirty-seven thousand people in the time of Evagoras I, and the island supported nine or ten kingdoms of very unequal size around it. The courts Hellenised fast, with Athenian orators addressing Cypriot kings and Greek craftsmen and physicians working on the island, while the population as a whole stayed mixed, Greek-speaking in most places, Phoenician at Kition, Eteocypriot at Amathus. Political violence was frequent, with revolts in 498, in the 390s and again in the 350s, and the kings' habit of changing sides means the same families appear as Persian loyalists and Greek champions within a single generation.

en: The Ptolemies worked the island as a royal estate, and the proceeds of its copper, timber and wine went to the treasury at Alexandria. Its forests kept the fleet in hulls, Cyprus being the main base of the Ptolemaic navy outside Egypt for close to two centuries, with the chief yard at Nea Paphos. Mints at Paphos and Salamis struck large quantities of Ptolemaic silver and bronze between about 200 and 80 BCE, the island being better supplied with silver than Egypt itself, and Athens and Alexandria were the steady partners in trade.

Koine Greek became the language of government, and the Greek alphabet finally displaced the Cypriot syllabary that had carried the island's Greek for some six centuries. The last securely dated syllabic inscriptions come from the rural shrine at Kafizin and belong to about 225 to 218 BCE, though some scholars would keep the script alive later still; the three hundred or so inscribed vessels dedicated there by a man named Onasagoras are mostly alphabetic, with a handful still syllabic or written in both scripts at once. Phoenician, the language of Kition's kings, went out with the dynasty Ptolemy I destroyed in 312 BCE, and the island's last Phoenician inscriptions are third century.

Aphrodite's sanctuary at Palaipaphos remained the greatest shrine on the island, its cult image not a statue but a tall conical black stone, and its chief priests were the Cinyradae. The Ptolemies added themselves to the pantheon: about thirty Cypriot inscriptions honour Arsinoe Philadelphus, many of them plain sandstone altars set up privately at Soloi, Chytroi, Idalion, Kourion and Salamis, and a text from Idalion dated 254 BCE names her eponymous priestess. By the late third century the strategos who governed Cyprus was also archiereus, high priest of the whole island, with its sanctuaries and their revenues in his hands.

Ptolemy I put an end to the city kingdoms: Pumayyaton of Kition was executed in 312 BCE, Stasioikos of Marion was arrested and his city destroyed with its people moved to Nea Paphos, and Nikokreon of Salamis was forced to take his own life in 311 or 310 BCE, the sources differing. Garrisons sat in every town under a single governor who was general and high priest together, residing first at Salamis and later at Nea Paphos, founded about 312 BCE and the first place to serve as capital of the entire island. No usable population figure survives for the period, and any number offered for Hellenistic Cyprus is a guess.

en: Copper was the island's name and its business: Roman aes cyprium, Cyprian metal, gave Latin cuprum and eventually the English word, and the hundred or so ancient slag heaps in the Troodos hold an estimated four million tonnes of waste, the by-product of perhaps 200,000 tonnes of metal smelted over some three thousand years on the geologist George Constantinou's reckoning. Radiocarbon dating puts the great red heap at Skouriotissa at between 73 and 26 BCE, and output there rose to a genuinely industrial scale in late antiquity. In 13 or 12 BCE Augustus gave Herod the Great half the revenue of the Cypriot mines and the management of the other half, a grant known only from Josephus; wine, olive oil, grain, timber, glass and shipbuilding filled out the trade, and provincial coin was struck at Paphos and Salamis.

Greek was the language of daily life and of nearly all writing, and the whole Roman period has left no more than about eighty Latin inscriptions on the island, a fair measure of how little Latin travelled beyond the governor's offices. The coinage tracks the shift neatly, issues under Augustus and Tiberius being in Latin, Claudian ones bilingual and everything after that in Greek. Paphos and the west kept an imperial calendar devised for Augustus, while Salamis went on using the Egyptian calendar it had inherited from the Ptolemies.

Three shrines held the right of asylum and Tacitus names them: Aphrodite at Paphos, Aphrodite at Amathus, and Zeus at Salamis, the first and last of which appear on the island's coins. Emperors were worshipped alongside the old gods rather than in temples of their own, and how much authority the koinon of Cyprus actually exercised over the island's religion is disputed among scholars. Christianity came early, Paul and Barnabas landing at Salamis about 45 CE and converting the proconsul Sergius Paulus at Paphos, though it spread slowly in the countryside; the Jewish revolt of 115 to 117 CE under Artemion wrecked Salamis and ended with the Jews expelled, Cassius Dio's figure of 240,000 dead being rhetoric rather than a count.

Cyprus became a senatorial province under a proconsul in 22 BCE with Nea Paphos as its capital, garrisoned so lightly that there is no evidence of anything beyond the governor's bodyguard. No reliable population figure exists for the province, though the theatre at Salamis seated some 15,000 and the city's necropolis sprawled across several square kilometres. Earthquakes shaped the age: the shock of 76 CE brought down three cities, which the ancient sources decline to name, and those of about 332 and 342 CE left Salamis and Paphos in ruins, after which Constantius II remitted four years of taxes and rebuilt Salamis on a smaller scale as Constantia.

en: Justinian's law of 536 detached Cyprus from the eastern prefecture and attached it to the quaestura exercitus, so that its grain, olive oil and wine went by sea to provision the Danube army, and the island's economy grew steadily more tied to Constantinople. Copper mining reached its peak here rather than its end: the exposed slag at Skouriotissa formed between about 320 and 520 CE, and Vasiliki Kassianidou has shown extraction surviving the Arab raids and continuing into the eighth century in the north west. Cypriot cooking pots from Dhiorios, made in something like factory conditions, were still reaching Palestine and even the Adriatic in the eighth century, which is the best evidence against the old picture of total collapse.

Greek replaced Latin in the imperial administration during the seventh century, and Cyprus followed the empire. Modern Cypriot Greek descends not from the ancient Arcadocypriot of the syllabary but from Byzantine medieval Greek, and its divergence is usually put down to the island being cut off from the rest of the Greek world between the seventh and tenth centuries; no vernacular Cypriot text survives from the period, so the early dialect is reconstructed rather than read. Arabic was present through the condominium and through the Maronite communities, some of whom were settled well before 1191, but no word in the dialect can be securely traced to that contact.

The Church of Cyprus won its independence from Antioch at the Council of Ephesus in 431, and the Quinisext Council of 692 confirmed it; when Justinian II moved the Cypriots to Nea Justinianoupolis near Cyzicus in 691 the archbishop kept his rank, and after the return in 698 or 699 he kept the title of Nea Justiniana and All Cyprus that his successors bear still. Tradition holds that Archbishop Anthemios found the tomb of Barnabas about 478 and that a grateful Emperor Zeno granted the archbishops the right to sign in red ink, wear imperial purple and carry a sceptre rather than a crosier, though Joseph Huffman has argued that these regalia privileges were in truth a sixteenth century construction. The condominium made the island a refuge during iconoclasm, and the great monasteries followed: Saint John Chrysostomos at Koutsovendis about 1070, Kykkos about 1100 under Alexios I, and Machairas, granted its whole mountain and stavropegial standing by Manuel I in 1172.

No scholarly population estimate for Byzantine Cyprus can be had, and the figures in circulation should be treated as guesses. Earthquakes struck Salamis in 332 and again ten years later, the second reportedly levelling whatever the sea had not taken, and Jerome found Paphos with nothing but ruins to show what it had been; the plague of Justinian is nowhere actually attested for the island, though Sir George Hill thought it inconceivable that Cyprus escaped. The Arab raids from 649 emptied the coast, Constantia being sacked and its people drifting to Famagusta while Kourion's survivors moved inland to Episkopi, and people came the other way too, with some 3,350 Armenian and Persian prisoners deported to the island under Maurice and Armenian troops settled after the reconquest of 965, although Luca Zavagno argues the destruction has been much overdrawn.

en: Sugar was the kingdom's great industry, grown and refined at Kouklia and Akhelia on the royal estates, at Kolossi under the Knights of Saint John and at Episkopi under the Venetian Cornaro, whose refinery employed four hundred hands in 1494; no sound export tonnage survives, though Pegolotti thought Cypriot sugar the best made anywhere and much of it went to the Martini house in Venice. Salt from the lake at Larnaca was a crown monopoly which every adult on the island was obliged to buy, raising some 80,000 besants a year in the 1390s and shipped on to Syria and Venice, while the camlet cloth woven by the women of Famagusta served as the very currency in which the kingdom paid its tribute, valued in Egypt at twenty ducats the piece. The fall of Acre in 1291 made Famagusta the chief entrepot of the Levant, its customs farmed in 1395 for 37,700 white besants, but the Genoese seizure of the port in 1373 and the Mamluk victory at Khirokitia in 1426, after which Janus was ransomed for 200,000 ducats and the island owed Cairo 5,000 ducats a year, broke the kingdom's finances for good.

French was the language of the court and of the Haute Cour, and the Assizes of Jerusalem were written in it before being turned into Greek in the fifteenth century and into Italian by 1531; Latin served the church and the charters, Italian rose with the Genoese and Venetians, and Greek remained the tongue of the great majority. The Cypriot Greek dialect became a literary language in its own right, Leontios Machairas writing his Recital concerning the Sweet Land of Cyprus in it in the 1420s and Georgios Boustronios carrying the story on to 1489, while a collection of Petrarchan sonnets in Cypriot Greek, once owned by the humanist Natale Conti and now in the Marciana at Venice, is the only known Petrarchism in the Greek language. Old French had its writers here too, chief among them Philippe de Novare, whose chronicle of the war against Frederick II survives inside the Gestes des Chiprois, and Guillaume de Machaut, who wrote nine thousand verses on Peter I's sack of Alexandria without ever setting foot on the island.

A Latin hierarchy was installed in 1196 with an archbishop at Nicosia and suffragans at Paphos, Limassol and Famagusta, and the settlements of 1220 and 1222 cut the Greek bishops to four and banished them to the villages of Solia, Arsinoe, Lefkara and Karpasia, agreements to which the Greeks were not even a party. Alexander IV's Bulla Cypria of 3 July 1260 made the Latin archbishop sole metropolitan and provided that after Germanos died the Greeks should have no archbishop at all, yet it also capped Latin visitation fees and left the Greek courts standing, which is why Chris Schabel has called it the Magna Carta of the Greeks; it governed the island until 1570. Coercion was rare but memorable, thirteen monks of the house of Kantariotissa being tried over the use of leavened bread in 1231, one dying in prison and twelve burned at Nicosia, an episode without parallel in the Latin east; the Maronites numbered perhaps seven or eight thousand in some thirty villages, the Armenians held a quarter of Nicosia still called Armenia, and the Nestorian merchants of Famagusta, the Lakhas brothers among them, built their own church there about 1360.

Gilles Grivaud, the standard authority, insists that no population count survives from the Lusignan period and that the curve cannot be drawn in absolute numbers; he works from a deliberately low figure of about 70,000 peasants for the royal accounts of 1412 and 1413, and rejects the 300,000 that circulates without evidence. Nine epidemics between 1347 and 1471 covered eighteen years in all, the Black Death of 1347 and 1348 costing between a third and two thirds of the people according to which chronicler one follows, though J. C. Russell's estimate of about twenty per cent is the sober corrective, and locusts stripped the crops for three or four years after 1409 until Janus ordered the eggs dug out and buried in 1413. Below a Frankish nobility that amounted to only a thousand or twelve hundred people in the thirteenth century sat the paroikoi, who owed two or three days' labour a week and a third of their crops and could be sold or flogged at their lord's will, then the perperiarii and the freed francomati; after Khirokitia the countryside rose in 1426 and a peasant styling himself King Alexis held Lefkoniko until he was hanged on 12 May 1427.
